title: Adders — from one bit to a four-bit sum
subtitle: Binary addition, the half and full adder, the ripple-carry chain, and the same circuit made to subtract. Every figure is a live logic circuit; every truth table is generated by simulating it.

intro.title: Introduction
intro.body:
A processor adds more often than it does anything else. Every loop counter, every array index, every multiply built from shifts and adds, every address the memory bus ever sees — all of it is addition. And the machine doing it has no concept of a number: it has wires that are either near the supply rail or near ground, and gates that combine them.

These notes build the adder up from that floor. First the four one-bit sums, then the half adder that produces them, then the full adder that can be chained, then a four-bit adder that carries a result from one stage to the next — and finally the same circuit made to subtract, and to drive a digit onto a display.

How to read these notesEvery circuit here is live. Each one carries its own Simulate button: press it and the logic solver runs that circuit, the output indicators show 0 or 1, and the sliders beneath change the inputs while it runs. A truth table under a figure is not typed out — it is produced by simulating that exact circuit for every input combination.
What this simulator does not model. Its logic pass settles instantly: it finds the stable value of every wire and stops. Real gates take time, and §9 is entirely about that time — but the figures there cannot show it, and the notes say so where it matters rather than pretending otherwise.

binary-sums.title: Adding two bits
binary-sums.body:
Binary addition has exactly four cases, and three of them are trivial. 0 + 0 is 0. 0 + 1 and 1 + 0 are both 1. The fourth case is where the hardware comes from: 1 + 1 is two, and two is not a digit in binary. It is written 10 — a 0 in this column and a 1 carried into the next.

So a one-bit adder cannot have one output. It needs two: the sum bit that stays in this column, and the carry bit that moves left. Everything else in this lesson follows from that single fact.
binary-sums.after: Four rows is the entire specification of a one-bit adder. The rest of this lesson is that specification implemented, chained, and then bent into doing subtraction.

half-adder.title: The half adder
half-adder.body:
Wire an XOR gate and an AND gate across the same two inputs and you have a half adder: the XOR produces the sum bit, the AND produces the carry. Two gates, two inputs, two outputs, and it implements Figure 2.1 completely.

The truth table under the circuit is not typed into these notes. It is generated by driving that exact circuit through all four input combinations and reading what comes out, so if the wiring were wrong the table would be wrong in the same way — which is the only kind of table worth printing beside a circuit.
half-adder.after:
Now try to use it. Adding two four-bit numbers means four columns, and every column but the rightmost has three bits arriving: the two input bits and the carry out of the column to its right. A half adder has two inputs. There is nowhere to put the carry.

That is what the name means. It is half of what a column of a real addition needs — and it is exactly right for the one column that has no carry coming in, the least significant.

ha-algebra.title: Reading the circuit off the truth table
ha-algebra.body: Figure 3.1 was presented as a finished circuit, which is the wrong way round: the table comes first and the gates are derived from it. Doing that derivation properly is the skill the rest of combinational design rests on.
ha-algebra.steps: A truth table with two outputs is two independent problems. The sum column and the carry column each get their own expression, and each is built from the rows where that output is 1 — the rows where it is 0 need no term, because a sum of products is 0 unless one of its products fires. Carry is 1 in exactly one row, A = 1 and B = 1. One row means one product term, and that term is the AND of the inputs in the state that row gives them. This is why the carry needs a single AND gate and nothing else. Sum is 1 in two rows: A = 0 with B = 1, and A = 1 with B = 0. Written directly as a sum of products, each row contributes the AND of its inputs with the 0s inverted. That expression — true when the inputs differ, false when they agree — is exclusive-OR, and a single gate implements it. Recognising a standard function in a sum of products is what turns four gates and two inverters into one, and it is worth doing before reaching for a Karnaugh map. Both outputs, from the same two inputs. Nothing is shared between them — the XOR and the AND look at the same wires and work independently, which is why both results appear at the same time.

full-adder.title: The full adder
full-adder.body:
A column in the middle of an addition receives three bits: A, B and the carry out of the column to its right. Their total runs from 0 to 3, which still fits in two output bits — a sum and a carry — so the shape of the circuit does not change. Only the input count does.

A circuit that adds three bits and produces a two-bit result is a full adder, and it is the unit every wider adder is built from. Three inputs means eight rows, and the table below is again generated by running the circuit rather than by asserting it.
full-adder.steps: The sum bit is 1 whenever an ODD number of inputs is 1 — rows 001, 010, 100 and 111. Odd-parity of several bits is chained XOR, so the two-input sum of the half adder simply extends. A carry leaves the column when at least two of the three inputs are 1. Written out one pair at a time, that is any of the three pairs being both-1. The two terms containing Cin share it, and A + B in that context is the same as A ⊕ B (the case where both are 1 is already covered by the AB term, so either spelling gives the same output). This form matters because it reuses the A ⊕ B the sum bit already computes — the same wire feeds both, which is what makes the two-half-adder construction of §6 possible.

fa-from-ha.title: A full adder from two half adders
fa-from-ha.body:
The factored carry expression, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), says something structural: everything a full adder needs is already produced by two half adders. The first adds A and B. The second adds that partial sum to the carry in. Each one hands over its own carry, and the two carries are ORed together.

The OR is safe because the two carries can never both be 1. If the first half adder carried, its sum bit was 0, so the second half adder had 0 + Cin and cannot carry. Only one of the two can fire in any row, which is why an OR — rather than a second adder — finishes the job.
fa-from-ha.after: Which one does hardware actually use? Neither shape is sacred. A standard-cell library implements the full adder as one optimised cell, chosen for its carry delay rather than its tidiness on paper, because the carry path is what sets the speed of everything built from it — which is §9.

ripple.title: The ripple-carry adder
ripple.body:
Chaining is now mechanical. One full adder per bit; each one's carry output becomes the next one's carry input; the rightmost carry input is 0, because nothing is carried into the least significant column. The carry out of the leftmost stage is the ninth bit of an eight-bit answer — or, for our four-bit adder, the fifth bit of a five-bit answer.

The circuit below adds A = 1011 (eleven) and B = 0110 (six). Seventeen does not fit in four bits, so the sum outputs read 0001 and the carry out reads 1: together, 10001, which is seventeen.

Set your own numbersPress Simulate, then use the eight sliders. A3 is the most significant bit of A and A0 the least; the same for B. Watch which output bits change when you flip A0 — a carry from the bottom can alter every bit above it.

worked-add.title: Worked example — 1011 + 0110
worked-add.body:
Add the two four-bit numbers of Figure 7.1 by hand, column by column, then check every bit against the circuit.

Each step is revealed one at a time. Work the column yourself before opening the next.
worked-add.steps: Column 0 (the least significant). A0 = 1, B0 = 0, and the carry in is 0 because nothing is carried into the rightmost column. One 1 among the three inputs: sum 1, no carry. Column 1. A1 = 1, B1 = 1, carry in 0. Two 1s: the total is two, which is 10 — the sum bit is 0 and a carry goes to column 2. Column 2. A2 = 0, B2 = 1, and now the carry in is 1. Two 1s again: sum 0, carry 1. This is the column where the ripple matters — its answer could not be computed until column 1 finished. Column 3 (the most significant). A3 = 1, B3 = 0, carry in 1. Two 1s: sum 0, and the carry leaves the adder entirely. Read the answer. The sum outputs spell 0001 and the carry out is 1, so the full five-bit result is 10001. In decimal that is 16 + 1 = 17, and 11 + 6 = 17 — the arithmetic checks. Check it against the circuit. Figure 7.1 reads S3 S2 S1 S0 = 0001 with the carry out at 1 — the same five bits, computed by four full adders rather than by hand. If your columns and the circuit ever disagree, the carry chain is where to look first: an error in column 1 silently poisons every column above it.

delay.title: Propagation delay and the carry path
delay.body:
Every gate takes time. Its output does not change at the instant its input does; it changes one propagation delay later, once the transistors inside have charged the next stage's input capacitance. Call that delay Δ and assume for now that every gate has the same one — a crude model, but the right one for comparing structures.

The sum outputs of a ripple-carry adder are not the problem. The carry is. It enters stage 0, leaves it, enters stage 1, and so on: the stages cannot work in parallel, because each one's answer depends on the one below it. The adder is not finished when its slowest gate is finished — it is finished when the carry has crossed every stage.
delay.steps: Every gate switches in Δ. The full adder is the two-half-adder circuit of §6, so its internal paths are: carry in to carry out passes an AND then an OR, which is 2Δ; an input A or B to carry out passes an XOR, an AND and an OR, which is 3Δ. These two numbers are the whole calculation. The equal-delay assumption is the approximation here — a real XOR is slower than a real NAND — and it is stated because everything below inherits it. Stage 0's carry comes from its own A and B inputs, so it appears 3Δ after the inputs are applied. That carry is what the rest of the chain waits for. From then on each stage only has to get an already-settled carry from its input to its output, which is the 2Δ path. Stage k's carry therefore appears 2Δ after stage k−1's. Add them up for an n-bit adder: 3Δ to produce the first carry, then 2Δ per stage for the remaining n−1 stages. The result is LINEAR in the width, which is the defining property of ripple-carry — and the reason it is abandoned for wide, fast datapaths.

overflow.title: Carry out, and what it does not tell you
overflow.body:
The carry out of the top stage answers one question: did the unsigned result need a fifth bit? For unsigned numbers that is the whole story — carry out 1 means the answer was too big for the width, and the value on the sum pins is the true answer modulo 16.

For signed numbers it is the wrong question. In two's complement the top bit is the sign, so a four-bit register holds −8 to +7, and the interesting failure is a result that leaves that range. Add 0111 (seven) and 0001 (one): the sum pins read 1000 and the carry out is 0. No carry left the adder, and the answer is still wrong — 1000 read as signed is −8.

The detector for signed overflow is different: overflow is the carry into the top stage disagreeing with the carry out of it, V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1. Equivalently, and more memorably: adding two numbers of the same sign and getting the opposite sign is always overflow, and adding opposite signs can never overflow.

subtractor.title: Subtraction without a subtractor
subtractor.body:
In two's complement, negating a number means inverting every bit and adding one. So A − B is A + (NOT B) + 1 — and an adder can do all of it, provided something can invert B on demand and something can supply the +1.

Both jobs are already available. An XOR gate with one input tied to a control line is a controlled inverter: with the control at 0 it passes its data input through unchanged, with the control at 1 it inverts it. And the +1 goes into the carry in of stage 0, the pin that was tied to 0 for plain addition.

One control line, called SUB, therefore turns a four-bit adder into a four-bit adder-subtractor: it feeds all four XOR gates and the carry in at once.
subtractor.after: Reading the carry out in subtract mode. It inverts its usual meaning: 1 means A ≥ B and the result is a plain positive number, while 0 means a borrow — the true answer is negative and the pins hold its two's-complement form. This is why processors distinguish 'carry' from 'borrow' in their documentation while using one physical flag for both.
subtractor.steps: Write down what subtraction becomes. Two’s complement turns A − B into an addition, so nothing new has to be computed: invert every bit of B, then add one. The circuit does the inversion with four XOR gates and the +1 with the carry in. Invert B. B = 0110, so each bit flips. This intermediate value is the one’s complement, and on its own it is not −6 — it is one short, which is what the next step supplies. Add, with the carry in at 1. Column 0: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so S0 = 1 and a carry goes up. Column 1: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, so S1 = 0, carry up. Column 2: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, so S2 = 1, no carry. Column 3: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, so S3 = 0 and the carry leaves the adder. Read the four sum bits. The fifth bit is the carry out and is not part of the numeric result — in subtract mode it is the borrow flag, and a 1 means no borrow was needed. Check both halves. 11 − 6 = 5, and the carry out of 1 confirms A ≥ B, so 0101 is a plain positive five rather than a two’s-complement pattern. Figure 11.2 reads exactly these five pins — 0101 with the carry out at 1. Drag its SUB slider to 0 and the same circuit returns 0001 with a carry out of 1, which is 11 + 6 = 17.

display.title: Putting the answer on a display
display.body:
Four sum bits are an answer only to someone who reads binary. A BCD-to-seven-segment driver turns a four-bit value into the seven segment signals that spell that digit, and a seven-segment display lights them.

The circuit below is the adder of §7 with its sum bits taken to a driver instead of stopping at the output pins: three plus four, and the display shows a 7. Nothing about the adder changed — the bits it produced were always a number; this is just the first figure that says so in a font.

Only one digit. A single display shows 0 to 9, and a four-bit adder can reach 15. Feed it 1010 or above and the driver has no digit to show — real designs convert the binary result to BCD first, with a converter that is itself built from adders.

problems.title: Problem set
problems.body: Six problems over the whole lesson. Work each on paper before opening its answer; where the answer can be settled by a circuit, it carries one you can run.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
Every circuit in this lesson was simulated, not asserted: the truth tables were generated by running the gates, and every figure's outputs were read off the solver. Six statements carry the rest.

  1. 1 + 1 = 10. A one-bit addition needs two outputs, a sum and a carry, and that is why adders exist at all.
  2. The half adder is S = A ⊕ B, C = A · B — complete for the least significant column, useless for any other, because it has no carry input.
  3. The full adder is S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), and it is exactly two half adders with their carries ORed.
  4. Ripple-carry chains them, one per bit, and costs (2n + 1) gate delays — linear in the width, which is why wide fast adders are built differently.
  5. The carry out answers the unsigned question only. Signed overflow is V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1: same-signed operands producing the opposite sign.
  6. Subtraction is free. Four XOR gates and the carry in turn the adder into an adder-subtractor, because A − B is A + NOT B + 1.
Next in this courseCarry-lookahead and fast adders: computing every carry directly from the inputs with generate and propagate terms, so the delay stops growing with the width — the answer to §9's 97.5 ns.
